乔治·惠特曼于1951年开办的书店，后来以“风滚草”待客传统闻名。经营方介绍，来: The bookshop George Whitman opened in 1951 later became known for its “Tumbleweeds” tradition of hospitality. Its operators describe writers, artists and travelers staying among the shelves, taking part in the shop’s life by reading, helping look after it and writing a one-page autobiography. A borrowed book may return, while a person who leaves might leave only a sheet of paper. These autobiographies become something like the bookshop’s own growing memory. The tradition gives today’s reader a concrete idea to consider: a literary meeting place is made not only by famous writers, but also by people who once made beds and tidied shelves here before they had made a name for themselves.

1982年的巴黎，餐桌也有座次: Paris in 1982: a table had its place in the hierarchy
同一家餐厅，一道楼梯曾被写成两种社交身份的分界。: In one restaurant, a staircase was described as a dividing line between two social positions.
1982年，《纽约时报》的一篇报道把Lipp写成了一幅巴黎社交剖面：有人在吧台喝: In 1982, a New York Times article portrayed Lipp as a cross-section of Parisian society: some people had a drink at the bar, others went upstairs, while regulars who knew the conventions cared deeply about a place downstairs. In the report, going upstairs meant more than moving to another room; it was like being pushed toward the edge of the social stage. Seats near the entrance carried connotations of visibility and status. The appeal of this story is how it brings things other than food into view: who is seen, who sits beside whom, and who can treat a particular place as a regular seat. At today’s entrance, you can read the observations preserved in that old report, but cannot expect the staff to arrange seating according to an account more than forty years old.

把椅子挪进树荫，是今天的自由；历史上，坐下还涉及一门生意。: Moving a chair into the shade is a freedom today; historically, sitting down was also a business.
卢森堡花园的椅子不只是风景的一部分。巴黎公园曾存在出租座椅的制度，收钱、发票、照: The Luxembourg Gardens’ chairs are more than part of the scenery. Parisian parks once had a chair-rental system, and collecting fees, issuing tickets and looking after the chairs was a dedicated job. People entering a garden for a walk had to deal with the chair attendant if they wanted to sit and rest. That detail reveals another history in an ordinary chair: whom a city allows to linger, and how it organizes comfort in public space. As you read today, notice how chairs face the pool and gather beneath the trees. The urban habit of making rest part of daily life is more interesting than memorizing a series of old ticket prices.

荷兰艺术家Jan Dibbets把纪念阿拉戈的作品铺进了巴黎的地面。这项1994: Dutch artist Jan Dibbets set his tribute to Arago into the ground of Paris. Completed in 1994, the work scattered bronze medallions marked ARAGO and with directional signs through the city along the Paris meridian. Arago was a French astronomer, physicist and participant in public affairs; the meridian reconnects his scientific work with the city. As you search for the medallions, you realize that this monument has no single front from which the whole can be gathered into one view. It asks to be discovered while walking. It is also contemporary art, not a mysterious ritual surviving from the Middle Ages.
